title: Airline booking
like: an airline's booking and seat system
brief: You run the booking system for an airline. Fare searches are heavy, seats are limited, and every flight needs the right number of tickets, no more and no fewer. You depend on a partner system for fares from other airlines, and it has strict limits. A fare sale and a slow partner will both happen on the same day.

clarify.q: Can two people hold the same seat?
clarify.a: Never. A seat is held by exactly one person, and holds expire after 15 minutes.

clarify.q: How heavy is a fare search?
clarify.a: Heavy. Most results can be reused for a few minutes, since fares move slowly, except during a sale.

clarify.q: What is the partner system limit?
clarify.a: About 200 requests a second, and during busy hours it can cut that in half without warning.
Passenger and payment records are sensitive. Every action must be audited, data encrypted, and backups proven to restore.

notes: About 3,500 fare searches a second at peak. Seat holds and changes are about 360 writes a second (approx.).
A partner (global distribution) system provides some fares; limit about 200 requests a second.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Fare searches per second at peak
Searches that reach the search index with a 90% cache hit rate
Seat holds, changes and payments per second

hints: Searching can use old answers. Holding a seat cannot. Where must the seat count live so two people cannot take the same one?

Keep seats in one strongly consistent database with synchronous copies. Cache fare searches for a few minutes so the partner system sees only a trickle, and wrap every outside call in a circuit breaker.

Balancer, 8 servers over 3 zones, a cache with a short keep time, a search index for own fares, a large primary with sync replication, circuit breakers on the partner API and payments, an idempotency store, a privacy vault, key service, audit log and backups.

editorial.summary: A seat is a scarce thing that two people want at once, so booking needs one strongly consistent truth. Everything around it can be fast and approximate: search, pages, notifications. The outside systems are the weak points, so every call to them gets a timeout, a breaker and a cache.

designs.name: One strong database, approximate everything around it
designs.why: A single large primary with synchronous copies makes every seat hold atomic. A search index and short cache absorb searches so the partner system is only asked for fares you cannot compute yourself. Circuit breakers keep a slow partner or payment company from taking the site with it.

designs.name: Distributed SQL across two regions
designs.why: Three nodes of a distributed SQL database stay correct if a whole zone is lost and can be spread across regions later. You pay about twice the database price and gain a path to running in two regions without changing how seats work.

tradeoffs: Sync replication adds a few ms to every seat hold. It is the reason a failover cannot lose a booking.
Caching fares for five minutes cuts partner calls by about 90 percent, and shows a price that may be a few minutes old. Re-check the price at checkout.
A circuit breaker returns "try again" quickly when the partner is slow. Without one, all your servers end up waiting on the partner.
Distributed SQL costs about twice as much per node and removes the single primary. A single big primary is simpler and cheaper until you need two regions.
The privacy vault and audit log are fixed costs. An audit failure costs more than both put together.
editorial.realWorld: Airlines hold their seat inventory in one authoritative system, and many fare lookups are answered from caches that are minutes old (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A 15-minute seat hold expires as payment succeeds. What seat schema and state transitions prevent two buyers from owning the seat?
correctness.discussion: Keep one authoritative row per flight or event and seat, with owner, hold token, expires_at and state. Acquire a 15-minute hold with an atomic conditional update. Move available to held to sold only if the buyer's token still owns an unexpired hold; the expiry worker must check that same token and state before releasing it. Enforce one sale per seat with a unique constraint. Charge using a stable payment idempotency key and reconcile unknown outcomes. If payment succeeds after the hold was lost, refund or void it instead of selling the seat again. Sync replication and a queue do not supply these transaction rules.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A durable copy across the required failure boundary before acknowledgement
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.
